Oil prices tumbled more than seven percent on Monday, the eve of crucial midterm elections in the United States, as signals that Tehran and Washington were renewing dialogue boosted hopes of ending the Middle East war.
Iran on Monday said "intensive" exchanges were underway with Washington and offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under strict conditions, as efforts escalated to avert a return to conflict.
Earlier, the Axios news outlet reported that US Vice President JD Vance had sent a letter to Iranian national security chief Mohsen Rezaei about possible new talks.
That was the highest-level move from President Donald Trump's administration in months.
Again Capital's John Kilduff described investors as experiencing "a violent change in market sentiment," adding that "we went from really, I think, expecting a major offensive after tomorrow's US elections to a potential breakthrough," he told AFP.
"All these losses will be taken right back if this doesn't pan out," Kilduff said.
The steep drop in oil prices translated into weakness among petroleum stocks. But Wall Street shares otherwise began the day with promise, bouncing back after last Friday's rout precipitated by worries over the tech industry's massive artificial intelligence spending.
But tech shares came under pressure as the session progressed, with the tech-focused Nasdaq slumping 1.1 percent.
"This is still a market that is on edge," said Joseph Zidle, chief market strategist at Cresset Capital, who described unease about midterm elections as adding to worries about the AI boom.
"The two of them are actually related," Zidle said of midterms and AI, noting that opposition to data centers has animated many campaigns.
AI has been "on the ballot in so many places, both blue and red," Zidle said. "It seems like data centers are part of the kitchen table issues."
Pollsters expect Democrats to win back control of the House of Representatives, but view Trump's Republican party as potentially able to maintain a majority in the Senate.
The loss of total Republican dominance would push the president into unfamiliar and uncomfortable territory: a lame duck period beset with high inflation at home, the sputtering war against Iran and hostile Democratic investigations into his activities in Washington.
"Investors are bracing for a fresh round of turbulence ahead of US midterm election fireworks while they assess the extent that companies are burning through cash to keep the AI bonfires burning," said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club.
Earnings this week will come from Apple, which reports after the close of trading on Monday, as well as Advanced Micro Devices and software titan Palantir will be closely watched this week. Shares in Apple fell 1.8 percent.

articles.title_orig: North Korea denies being behind record $6.3bn Binance hack
articles.title_zh: North Korea denies being behind record $6.3bn Binance hack
articles.content_orig:
North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance , calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric".
Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un , said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history.
This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy.
Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor.
The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group.
"The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement.
"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said.
But Pyongyang has been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks in recent years - accusations that it has denied.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said.
The country has consistently denied such claims.
Kim Yo Jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace".
The BBC has contacted Binance for comment. Since the hack, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users.
The company said last week that initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals.
Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack.
A net $5.27bn has been withdrawn from the exchange since transactions resumed on Sunday, according to data posted on Tuesday by Binance. It also said the level of transactions has now stabilised.
The company has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack and that it has so far covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach.

In this keynote at the Aristotle-Confucius Symposium in Varanasi, economist Jeffrey Sachs traces how Asia’s share of world production fell under European and American imperialism and why it is now returning to the center of the global economy. He talks about India-China ties, the rise of a multipolar world, family businesses and corporate responsibility, reviving the United Nations, and why the shared ethics of the world’s great traditions can help build a new world order of peace and cooperation. Read the full transcript of this lecture below:

Doctor Adani, thank you for that brilliant address, but especially for all that you and your family and the foundation are doing for the world, which is very profound and very moving also to hear. And, Nirupam, thank you for the last thirty two years of collaboration and the continuing thirty two years of collaboration at least. I’m thrilled with all that we do together and most grateful. I want to thank the government of India, the Ministry of Culture.
I know the Secretary of Culture will be arriving shortly. His plane was diverted because of the fog this morning, but I think he’s landed and will arrive soon. I want to thank the partnership, of course, of the Adani Foundation and the Adani Group. And to pay my great respect to what the Adani Group is doing for sustainable development in India and globally because the scale of your work is remarkable as you just described, and it’s very, very inspiring. I’d like to thank TERI, which is a partner in organizing this symposium.
With TERI, we go back many decades of TERI’s leadership in sustainable development and in green energy and in climate safety. So it’s a tremendous joy to be working with TERI and joining together with TERI.
For me, it’s very moving to be here in Varanasi. Sonia and I first came here forty seven years ago. We fell in love with this magical place, which is one of the great, most holy places on the planet and one of the greatest centers of learning and knowledge and spirituality in the world, there’s probably not another place that combines such crucial world traditions as the place where we are.
So to be in Varanasi is absolutely extraordinary. We keep coming back, and we are inspired every time that we come together. And for me, it’s wonderful that so many of our colleagues and friends from this effort of ancient wisdom for modern challenges are together again here so that we can add, I think, significantly and profoundly to the depth of our work together and to help advance that work.
I’d like to spend a few minutes on the background of this symposium and why I think it’s so important. I have prepared remarks, which I will share with anyone that’s interested later, but I will not read them certainly right now.
I want to just share some basic thoughts with you. And I do need one slide, this one. So a lot of numbers, but the numbers… I’m an economist. I can’t help but look at some numbers.
But the numbers, I think, are absolutely key to understanding our world today. We are in a new territory in the world, not only because of AI or because of climate change or because of other technological disruptions that we face or being in the nuclear age, which is sad to say, perhaps the deepest reality of our world, which is the capacity to… Of humanity to end humanity in about seventy minutes as the current analyses show.
But we’re in a different world because history has moved in a very important and fundamental way, and that’s what these numbers help us to understand. So what you see here for several benchmark years starting in 1700 at the top row and then going to projections to 2100 to the end of the twenty first century in the bottom row, our estimates of the share of world production, this is a shorthand, but the share of the world product produced in different regions of the world.
And I’m showing you The United States, Europe, which in this case is the European Union plus Great Britain, China, and India. And I want you to see what has happened in history and what is happening today. Back in 1700, China and India each had about 20% of world production. Europe, about 24%. The United States didn’t exist yet.
It wouldn’t exist till the end of the example very to see be so of how that we’re world. The world economy. There’s obviously other places of not counted in this table to add up to a 100%.
As late as 1800, China was a third of world output more than Europe. India had already started to lose its share because India was already starting to be imperialized by Britain and by other European empires, which would be soon kicked out by Britain.
But India was being held back by the British Empire. China, not yet. It had not faced yet British imperialism that was to come starting in 1839. The United States now existed, and it was 1% of world output.
By 1900, the world had changed fundamentally because the nineteenth century was the century in which Europe temporarily dominated the world, and that was the world of European empire, not centuries long a century of domination of the nineteenth century.
And in that nineteenth century, of course, India fell entirely under British rule. China entered into what China calls the “century of humiliation,” which began with the… One of the most sordid wars of history, the war by Britain on China to force China to open up to actually British grown, India grown opium. It’s hard to imagine a more disgusting war than this, although I think the current Iran war ranks high as well, a war out of nothing.
But the Opium Wars started a century of disaster for China because two Opium Wars were followed by a massive civil war in China after those disruptions, known to us as the Taiping Rebellion, but really one of the largest civil wars in history.
And to cap that off at the end of the nineteenth century, Japan invaded China and began forty years of invasions of China so that there was catastrophe in both India and China.
Millions of people died in repeated famines in India completely unrelieved by the British Empire who stuck with a stiff upper lip to their laissez faire policy as people were dying and continued to export grains from famine stricken regions of this country.
So by 1900, Europe’s share of the world output was almost 40%. China and India together, and, of course, India being part of the British empire at that point, were now less than 20%.
So a decline to a mere 18% of world output for two countries that held more than 40% of the world population. 1950 was the nadir of Asia because this was a hundred fifty years of European and then American imperialism with American overseas imperialism starting in the eighteen nineties, first overthrowing the Kingdom of Hawaii and then taking the colony of The Philippines in the so called Spanish-American War.
Look at the situation in 1950. 56% of world output was in The United States and Europe, more than half. Whereas in China and India now combined on the independence of India and the independence of the People’s Republic Of China under 10% combined for two countries which still constituted more than 40% of world output.
That world of 1950 and the world that was created between 1800 and 1950 came to be seen as the norm of the world, that the West leads the world, the West designs the global realities, Asia is a small footnote under Western guidance, and this ideology was the prevailing ideology of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. articles.title_orig: Indian national killed after two helicopters collide in Nepal's Mount Everest region
articles.title_zh: Indian national killed after two helicopters collide in Nepal's Mount Everest region
articles.content_orig:
An Indian tourist was killed when two helicopters collided in Nepal's Everest region on Tuesday, police said.
The collision occurred after the helicopters' rotor blades struck each other as they were landing at the Pheriche helipad at around 8:11 am local time (0226 GMT), assistant sub-inspector Mukesh Singh told dpa.
The 47-year-old man from the southern Indian state of Tamil Nadu was a passenger aboard a Fishtail Air helicopter carrying two passengers and a pilot. He died at the scene, while the other passenger, a New Zealander, was airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment, Singh said.
Nepal has experienced dozens of aviation accidents in recent years, largely attributed to its challenging terrain and poor aviation safety record.
Nepal, home to eight of the world's 14 highest peaks, is currently in its autumn season, which is considered one of the best times for trekking and hiking in the country, including in the Everest region.

articles.title_orig: Baked by Melissa enters Target with first at-home cupcake mix
articles.title_zh: Baked by Melissa enters Target with first at-home cupcake mix
articles.content_orig:
Baked by Melissa will enter the at-home baking aisle in Target stores as the retailer tries to persuade shoppers to spend more at its locations this holiday season.
As of Sunday, Target is exclusively selling the brand's cupcake kits, liners and a cupcake pan, all in the dessert company's signature bite-size portions. The line includes three cupcake flavors: Christmas Tie-Dye, Marshmallow Hot Cocoa and Red Velvet.
The company's entry into at-home baking comes as a number of restaurants turn to consumer packaged goods to boost sales in an otherwise challenging time for the industry.
Some players, such as California Pizza Kitchen and TGI Fridays, have licensed their brands for frozen foods for decades. But other restaurant chains, including Chick-fil-A and Dutch Bros , have leaned into grocery products much more recently. For smaller companies, such as Momofuku or Carbone , space on a grocery shelf helps extend brand reach and gives consumers a chance to try their food without a reservation and at a much lower cost.
Founded by Melissa Ben-Ishay in 2008, Baked by Melissa has nine permanent locations in the New York area and ships its minicupcakes nationwide.
The regional chain has garnered attention outside the city thanks to Ben-Ishay's social media presence. On TikTok, the Baked by Melissa account has more than 2.8 million followers, fueled by popular recipe videos, such as for her green goddess salad dressing. Ben-Ishay's social media stardom has led to collaborations with Ferrero and Wonder .
Baked by Melissa had discussed at-home baking products for years, but Ben-Ishay only decided to take the plunge a year ago during a trip to Target with her two kids, she told CNBC. A spin through the baking aisle made her decide Baked by Melissa "should be here," she said.
"I love baking cake mix. I truly do. And, quite frankly, sometimes I just think it tastes better," Ben-Ishay said.
But retail moves more slowly than Baked by Melissa's usual pace.
The dessert company needed just a few days to create New York Knicks-branded minicupcakes after the team won the NBA championship in June, for example, but figuring out retail products meant "a lot of waiting and approvals and new partners," Ben-Ishay said.
Twelve months later, the cupcake mixes have arrived on store shelves, just in time for the all-important holiday season.
For Target, the next two months will be critical as the retailer tries to woo back its core customer after a disappointing holiday season last year. That prototypical Target shopper often looks a lot like Ben-Ishay.
"We started with Target because I'm a 42-year-old mom of two, and I find myself there a lot," she said.

articles.title_orig: UK to double wait for permanent residency, with exemptions for care workers
articles.title_zh: UK to double wait for permanent residency, with exemptions for care workers
articles.content_orig:
Al Jazeera investigation exposes paramilitary hitman linked to Turning Point UK
The United Kingdom has revised its immigration rules, doubling the time most foreign workers must wait to qualify for permanent residency to 10 years and making refugees who arrive on “small boats” wait as long as 30 years.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, speaking in Parliament on Monday, said hundreds of thousands of care workers will be exempt from the hardline rules, offering a concession amid a political outcry within the governing Labour Party.
Permanent residency, known in the UK as indefinite leave to remain, carries the right to work, study, use the free National Health Service and claim welfare benefits. Until now, it has been granted after five years.
The new rules, set to take effect next year, tie eligibility for permanent residency to income.
People who earn more than 50,000 pounds a year ($67,000) will still be able to apply after five years, and those earning more than 125,000 pounds ($167,500) after three. Everyone else will be placed on the 10-year path. The median salary in the UK is about 39,000 pounds (roughly $52,000).
The rules will apply retroactively to workers already in the country.
“Settlement should not be automatic. It should be earned,” Mahmood, the home secretary, told Parliament, adding that the changes would restore fairness by linking the right to settle to what immigrants contribute.
“Those who contribute most will settle fastest,” she said. “Those who don’t play by the rules will be refused or wait longer.”
The UK government first proposed last year that lower-skilled workers wait 10 to 15 years for permanent residency.
But the plan drew fierce opposition from unions and parts of the Labour Party, particularly over its effect on care workers, who are often poorly paid and work in a sector that has long struggled to fill vacancies. Many of them arrived in the early 2020s, as the country was reeling from the COVID-19 pandemic, to fill gaps left by European workers who had departed after Brexit.
Under the revised plan, care workers will be able to settle after five years if they have met the conditions of their visas and earn at least 25,000 pounds ($33,500) a year.
Mahmood said the rules would offer a path for care workers “who worked hard and answered our call when we needed them”.
As for refugees, those who arrive through one of the government’s “new safe and legal routes” will be able to settle after five years, she said. For other refugees, the standard wait will become 20 years, reduced to 10 years for those who work or study. Anyone who arrived by an “illegal method”, such as by small boat, could wait up to 30 years for settlement, she said.
Under the new rules, applicants will also be disqualified if they have a criminal record, cannot speak English “to a high standard”, owe money to the government, or have not made at least three years of national insurance contributions.
Mahmood said the overhaul would mean that half a million people would settle later than they otherwise would have, saving the government billions of pounds in benefits.
In total, the government estimates that as many as 1.4 million people will receive settled status between 2026 and 2030.
The changes, announced after a 12-week public consultation that drew more than 200,000 responses, are part of a broader effort to tighten immigration rules after arrivals surged following Brexit.
They are a response to political pressure, including from Nigel Farage’s populist Reform UK party, which has surged in popularity in recent years with calls for stricter migration controls. Reform UK has sought to depict the arrivals of refugees on small boats across the English Channel as a crisis, and anti-immigration activists have staged protests, including outside facilities that house asylum seekers.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government has said that increased law enforcement cooperation between the UK and France has helped reduce the number of people making the crossing so far this year by more than 40 percent compared with 2025.

articles.title_orig: Gas prices are set to be highest for any Election Day in U.S. history
articles.title_zh: Gas prices are set to be highest for any Election Day in U.S. history
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump promised voters angry about inflation that he would slash gas prices below $2 a gallon within his first year in office.
"My plan will cut energy prices in half or more than that within 12 months of taking office," Trump said in a speech to the New York Economic Club in September 2024 during his re-election campaign.
"Energy was what caused our problem initially," he told voters. "Energy is going to bring us back. That means we're going down and getting gasoline below $2 a gallon."
But when voters head to the ballot box on Tuesday energy prices will remain a headache. Gas and diesel prices are forecast to be the highest ever on an election day, according to Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy.
"Prices have never been this high this late in the year," De Haan said.
Gas prices stood at a national average of $4.20 a gallon on Friday, nearly 40% above the same period last year. The price of diesel, critical to transportation and agriculture, has surged about 70% over the past year, to $6.32 a gallon.
During the 2022 U.S. midterm elections, the year that Russia invaded Ukraine and triggered an energy crisis, retail gas prices stood at $3.80, according to AAA data.
"Trump got in his own way," De Haan said. "Back in December, we predicted that 2026 was going to be the cheapest year for gas since 2020. That required no effort. And obviously, it hasn't gone that way."
Fuel prices have spiked since Trump decided to attack Iran in a joint attack with Israel on Feb. 28. Tehran retaliated with a wave of strikes on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, severely depressing oil flows through the vital shipping route.
Trump told voters at a rally in Michigan last Sunday that rising fuel prices are a "small price to pay" to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.
"Once this conflict comes to an end, gas prices will drop drastically, and the Iranian terrorist regime will not have a nuclear weapon," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement.
The White House said gas prices when adjusted for inflation have been higher around previous election days.
Exports through Hormuz have rebounded since the summer as the U.S. military helped ships through the strait. But the Middle East disruption has been compounded by Houthi rebel attacks on Saudi Arabian refineries, and Ukraine's strikes on refineries in Russia. Trump had promised to end that war in the first week of his second term, but the conflict is stuck in an intractable stalemate.
"Frankly, diesel is the key crunch point here because it is so critical to economic growth," ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods told CNBC on Friday after the nation's largest oil company posted huge profits thanks to the disruptions.
Airlines have hiked their fares to cover high costs from jet fuel, their biggest expense other than labor, hurting the fight to contain inflation.
Trump came under political pressure from Republicans to take action on fuel prices ahead of Tuesday's election. The cost of diesel is hurting big farm states like Iowa that have overwhelmingly backed Trump in his presidential campaigns. The senate race in the Hawkeye State has become competitive.
Trump briefly contemplated a diesel export ban as Senator Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) lobbied to help the state's farmers. The president decided against it because it might also have raised gasoline prices.
Instead, Trump issued an executive order to allow truckers to use tax-exempt, offroad diesel on U.S. highways, and announced an $8 billion relief program for farmers hit by high fuel prices.
Trump later struck a controversial deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Moscow to export about 6 million barrels of diesel into the global market through November.
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and even some Republican senators slammed the agreement as rewarding Russian aggression. Energy analysts said the diesel volumes in the Russia deal are small compared to global demand and won't have a meaningful impact on prices.
More recently, crude oil prices have rallied ahead of the election. Trump has said he will not resume strikes on Iran before the midterms. But the market is pricing in the risk of another round of fighting after voting ends on Tuesday. International Brent crude oil prices are up more than 13% in October and U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude is up 15%.
"If there are escalations, that could obviously put upward pressure on prices just ahead of Thanksgiving," De Haan said, "which is also when Americans have really staunch traditions in terms of driving to friends and family."

articles.title_orig: China expands swap and relending tools to steady the stock market
articles.title_zh: China expands swap and relending tools to steady the stock market
articles.content_orig:
China's central bank said it will run swap operations for brokers, fund managers and insurers as conditions warrant, pull in more participants, and trim the fees charged for those swaps. Alongside that, it will lower the interest rate on its relending program tied to share repurchases and stake building to 1% from 1.25%, make that facility a standing feature, and press banks to extend more credit through it.
Both tools debuted in October 2024. The relending channel supplies cheap central bank funding that banks use to make loans backing listed companies and major shareholders who are buying back stock or adding to stakes.
According to the securities regulator, the next swap tranche is expected to start shortly, and 31 approved brokerages and fund managers are together applying for quotas exceeding 100 billion yuan, or about $15 billion. The latest tally from the central bank shows swaps outstanding at 105 billion yuan, while roughly 440 billion yuan in loans tied to buybacks and stake-raising have been signed and over 280 billion yuan has already been paid out.
A meeting on the measures drew 23 securities firms and funds and 26 banks. Speakers included representatives from China International Capital Corp., Guotai Haitong Securities Co., Citic Securities Co., Industrial & Commercial Bank of China Ltd., China Construction Bank Corp. and China Citic Bank Corp.

Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout.
The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an investor day last week , shares tumbled 8.8% Monday.
"This seems to be exactly what they previewed," said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. "So I'm not sure why the market is freaking about it."
Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments.
The hyperscaler's stock initially bounced after last Wednesday's investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was limiting its additional capital market funding for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion.
"This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated)," UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday.
Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028.
Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of Aug. 31, with the bulk in senior notes.
What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday.
"Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space," he said. "If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of '27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out."

articles.title_orig: Australia hikes rates to 18-year high to fight inflation
articles.title_zh: Australia hikes rates to 18-year high to fight inflation
articles.content_orig:
Australia's central bank raised its benchmark cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on Tuesday, the highest level since November 2008.
The Reserve Bank of Australia's move was in line with expectations from economists polled by Reuters, and marked its fifth rate increase this year.
In its statement, the RBA said that the move was a split decision, with six members voting for the increase and three opting for a hold.
This also comes as the country continues to grapple with high inflation, with the consumer price index rising 4.3% in September, up from 4% in August and marking its highest level since March.
The central bank also said inflation is now expected to "remain elevated through much of 2027," and not expected to fall back into its 2%-3% target range till late 2027, three quarters later than previously forecast.
This was due to higher fuel and other commodity prices, in addition to factors including AI-related investment, which is driving rapid growth in prices for technology-related goods, the RBA said.
In its September decision, RBA governor Michelle Bullock said that inflation is "too high," driven by higher oil prices from the Iran War and stronger domestic spending.
"We're seeing signs that upside risks to inflation are materializing," she added, saying that additional hikes will come "if that's what's needed to get inflation down."
Growth has slowed in the first two quarters of 2026. Australia's GDP rose 2.1% in the June quarter compared to a year earlier, down from 2.5% in the March quarter.
The RBA is trying to bring inflation back under control while higher borrowing costs and cost-of-living pressures weigh on households and activity.
When asked if she sees a recession for Australia, Bullock said that it is "not our base case at the moment."

articles.title_orig: Russian attack on Ukraine aid hub kills 26 as US announces new peace talks
articles.title_zh: Russian attack on Ukraine aid hub kills 26 as US announces new peace talks
articles.content_orig:
Russian air strikes kill at least 26 in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region
Russian forces have bombed an aid centre in Ukraine, killing at least 26 people, according to Ukrainian officials, as the United States announced plans for new peace talks on November 10 and 11.
The aid centre, at a school in the village of Komyshuvakha in the Zaporizhzhia region, had been closed to students because the village sits too close to the front line, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday. Instead, it served as a shelter and as a weekly distribution point for aid packages, which residents who remain in the village collected every Monday.
“The Russians struck first just as people were arriving – a few aerial bombs,” he said in his nightly address. “Then there was a second strike – more air bombs, this time on the shelter. A vile terrorist strike.”
Zelenskyy said the Russians could not have been unaware that residents remaining in Komyshuvakha gathered each week to pick up humanitarian packages.
Among the dead were two members of a rescue crew and four police officers, according to Ukraine’s emergency services. Five people, including two rescue workers, were being treated in hospitals. Regina Kharchenko, the secretary of the Zaporizhzhia City Council, said 27 people were missing, and regional police said officers and rescuers were working to reach residents believed to be trapped under the rubble.
Photographs posted online showed smouldering debris scattered across the area.
There was no immediate comment from Russia.
Zelenskyy said Russian forces could not have been unaware of the weekly aid gatherings.
“This is yet further proof that Russia does not want any kind of de-escalation, any real justice,” Zelenskyy said.
He argued that Moscow had squandered an opening created by a humanitarian mission last week in Oleshky , a Russian-occupied southern city, which was brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.
“If Russia genuinely wanted de-escalation, there was an opportunity following the situation in Oleshky to continue taking humanitarian steps,” he said. “We proposed this. But Russia continues to kill people.”
Zelenskyy also said Ukrainian intelligence had warned that Russia was preparing a new “massive attack” on the country’s energy and logistics networks, timed to coincide with the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
Writing on X, he said Moscow was counting on the world’s attention being elsewhere, allowing Ukraine’s struggles with air defences and Patriot missiles to go unnoticed.
He urged Washington to pressure Russia “in such a way that it has no alternative but to end this war”.
Hours after the attack, US special envoy Steve Witkoff said that delegations from Ukraine and Russia would meet in Abu Dhabi, in the United Arab Emirates, on November 10 and 11.
In a social media post, Witkoff said the talks would address “post-war security agreements, de-escalation, humanitarian measures, and ending the war”.
Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to the new round of three-way talks after meeting Witkoff in St Petersburg on October 21.
The talks come as US negotiators seek a breakthrough before winter in the war, now in its fifth year.
The last US-mediated talks were held in February, before the US and Israel launched their war on Iran.
Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, cited Monday’s attack in urging countries to oppose Russia’s return to elite international sport, after the Court of Arbitration for Sport ordered that Russia be reinstated in major ice hockey tournaments.
“Russia deserves condemnation, isolation, and consequences, not a return to international respectability,” Sybiha wrote on X.
Elsewhere in Ukraine on Monday, drone strikes injured 12 people in the eastern Kharkiv region, damaging a refrigeration facility, greenhouses and homes, according to emergency services. In the Black Sea port of Odesa, five people were injured when a warehouse was hit and nearby houses were damaged.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said its forces had shot down 212 Ukrainian drones overnight. The governor of Russia’s Samara region, Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, said air defences had repelled an attack there but gave no further details.

articles.title_orig: Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal
articles.title_zh: Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump has notified Congress of his intention to remove South Africa and Rwanda from a preferential trade programme, from 1 January 2027.
The African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa) allows eligible African countries to export thousands of products to the US duty-free.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement that an annual review had found that both countries were engaging in practices inconsistent with the programme's eligibility requirements.
He added that the Trump administration had additionally notified the two countries of the decision.
The Trump administration cited barriers to US trade and investment, as well as concerns over national security and foreign policy interests in the region.
In Rwanda's case, Washington also raised concerns about human rights, political pluralism, the rule of law and workers' rights.
The move comes barely a week after Rwanda's defence ministry was hit with sanctions by US Treasury for its alleged role in the armed rebellion in eastern DR Congo.
The US Treasury said Rwanda's defence ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 rebels in eastern DR Congo, providing weapons, equipment, logistics and training.
For South Africa, the US additionally pointed to corruption.
"The Trump administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria," Greer said.
South Africa's trade Minister Parks Tau described the decision as "unfortunate", saying Washington was raising new issues that had not featured in trade negotiations between the two countries which began in 2025.
"We will continue to accelerate the diversification of South Africa's export markets to protect jobs," Tau said.
US Ambassador to South Africa Leo Brent Bozell III said it was regrettable that South African policies led to its termination from Agoa.
"This was a predictable and preventable outcome resulting from the rejection by South Africa's government of real concerns raised by the US," he wrote on X.
The announcement comes amid strained relations between Washington and both countries, with the proposed termination threatening their access to preferential trade arrangements with the US.
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.

1) Choose which competitor you'd like to use instead. If you want to stop streaming altogether, buying albums directly off Bandcamp is a great way to support an artist directly. If you can't shake your dependency on streaming catalogues, there are plenty of alternatives like Tidal, Apple Music and Qobuz. I would not recommend Amazon or YouTube Music for both obvious (both companies suck) and technical reasons (they're bad apps, and YT Music has terrible sound quality).
2) If your new service supports it directly (Apple Music on iOS does, for example), you can sometimes just transfer your Spotify library straight over. If it doesn't, you can use a service like Free Your Music or TuneMyMusic , which might cost you a few bucks but in the grand scheme of things is worth the investment. Those tools will do their best (and by experience they're very good) at moving your whole library, playlists and all, off Spotify and over to your new platform of choice. If you also listened to podcasts within Spotify, most rivals will also offer podcasts within their music app, but if they don't--Android users can't use Apple Podcasts, for example--Pocket Casts is a totally workable solution.

articles.title_orig: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
articles.title_zh: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
articles.content_orig:
Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.
A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co. , a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “ XCPE ” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).
The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.
The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year , residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.
“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”
The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems .
Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).
The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt , also known as Honeygain , which is owned by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs . In October 2026, Oxylabs was relaunched under a new brand called Source , after receiving $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion. Oxylabs did not respond to a request for comment.
Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut , a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies . In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut , saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM , Traffmonetizer , Jaguar , LINKFOG , BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode .
Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient , a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks . Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.
Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.
In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology , concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.
The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.
Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass . In our November 2025 story, “ Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet? ” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.
That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.
Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was mentioned in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linux Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers [Linux Tech Tips said in a statement shared with Synthient that it has since updated the video to explicitly frame the product as a scam and have removed all associated affiliate links].
The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.
The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”
Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”
“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

articles.title_orig: Asian stocks retreat ahead of US midterms, oil steadies
articles.title_zh: Asian stocks retreat ahead of US midterms, oil steadies
articles.content_orig:
Markets are sweating it out ahead of the midterm elections, but the event historically heralds strong performance for stocks — regardless of whether it's a red or blue wave, split decision, or status quo in Washington.
The S&P 500 tends to perform well after both midterm and presidential elections. According to a CNBC analysis of S&P 500 returns after elections from 1980 through 2024, the index rose an average of 0.2% after one day and one week, and 1.1% after one month across both presidential and midterm elections.
A year later, the index gained an average of 13.7% after midterms and 13.8% after presidential elections. Returns were positive in 91% of cases. And the S&P 500 was up after all 11 midterms from 1982 through 2022.
Short-term returns were less reliable, particularly after presidential contests, which produced slightly negative average returns after one day and one week.
"There's some anxiousness before these elections," Ryan Detrick, CNBC contributor and chief market strategist at Carson Group, told CNBC. "Once you are through it, it's a big relief and markets tend to do pretty well."
Still, the market usually prefers divided government: one party in charge of the White House and the other holding at least one house of Congress.
Across 10 midterm and five presidential elections that left no single party in charge, the S&P 500 rose an average 15% after one year. One-year returns were positive in 14 out of 15 cases. By comparison, the index gained an average of 11.5% over the year after elections that resulted in single-party control.
"If you have a huge red wave or a big blue wave, markets actually kind of don't like that as much because you have too much spending one way and too much power," Detrick said.
Leaving Democrats in control of Congress with a Republican in the White House — a scenario that may emerge from the elections on Tuesday — was also positive. A CNBC analysis found that after the three midterms (1986, 1990 and 2006) when Democrats controlled both houses and a Republican held the presidency, the S&P 500 averaged a 0.5% decline on the reaction day but was up 3.4% a month later and 10.9% after a year.
Granted, elections may be coincident events to factors that matter far more for market performance.
The S&P 500 plunged 22.1% in the year after the 2000 elections due to the dotcom bust, marking the worst post-election performance since 1980. Conversely, the S&P 500's best post-election year was a 38.3% gain after the 2020 elections, when markets mounted a massive comeback from the COVID-induced selloff.
Investors should bear in mind that Federal Reserve policy and the corporate earnings cycle ultimately matter more than elections, according to Société Générale.
Stocks declined in the aftermath of the 2018 midterms, for instance, when Democrats wrested control of the House during President Donald Trump's first term. More importantly, the Fed tightened monetary policy that year, raising interest rates four times, and the S&P 500 ended the year down 6.2%, though the market was up 11.7% a year after the election.
The big swing factor now is AI and whether declines in tech will continue. As long as the AI wave is still moving and the economy keeps growing, "this bull market is probably still alive and well," Detrick says.
But a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate would almost certainly pressure the AI infrastructure buildout and could lead to more retrenchment.
The bond market is also skittish with yields rising globally and a mini debt crisis in France. And the war with Iran could get worse post-election if President Trump follows through on threats of more strikes or Iran escalates.
"Seasonality isn't destiny, and worries around Iran, AI and France won't mysteriously vanish," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note.
If history is any guide, we could see a Santa rally and S&P 500 gains after the midterms. But this is still an AI-driven market, with geopolitics, the Fed, and bond market very much in charge.
— CNBC's Chris Hayes contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: More grocery stores in Europe report fridge and freezer temperature spikes as apparent cyberattacks continue
articles.title_zh: More grocery stores in Europe report fridge and freezer temperature spikes as apparent cyberattacks continue
articles.content_orig:
Grocery store chains in at least three European countries reported unexpected temperature spikes Monday in refrigerators and freezers that ruined food — the second time in less than a month that similar incidents have raised concerns about cyberattacks on increasingly interlinked infrastructure.
Netherlands-based food retailer Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt in Belgium both said an IT incident overnight had sent temperatures inside fridges and freezers in dozens of their stores in Belgium and Luxembourg soaring, while Swedish chains ICA and Coop reported similar spikes, with one outlet explicitly blaming a cyberattack, according to the Reuters news agency.
The incidents come less than three weeks after several French supermarket chains said they were hit by a cyberattack that sent refrigerator temperatures surging as high as 122 degrees Fahrenheit in hundreds of outlets.
French chains E. Leclerc, Intermarché and Cooperative U told the AFP news agency last month that they had suffered a cyberattack.
On Monday, Reuters said Ahold, the Dutch grocery store chain, had reported a cybersecurity incident to police in the Netherlands in October after detecting suspicious activity in its infrastructure. The chain realized there were temperature increases in the cooling systems on Monday, Delhaize spokesperson Sarah De Meester told Reuters.
The CEO of Belgian refrigeration company Sabcobel, which operates the systems used by Delhaize and other chains, told Belgium's national Belga news agency a cyberattack was to blame after fridge and freezer units' evaporators were switched into defrost mode.
"We began mobilizing technicians at 1 a.m. to get the situation under control," Stephan Moelans told Belga. "We've been working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network."
"Over the past few weeks, we've been working very hard to protect our customers' fridges against this vulnerability," he told the news agency, but he added that many units would require physical modifications, and "that requires investment."
A handful of Swedish supermarkets also saw refrigerator and freezer temperatures soar early Monday, two chains said, forcing them to throw away spoiled food. ICA and Coop both told AFP they had no immediate information about their systems being subjected to a cyberattack.
ICA told AFP "a limited number" of its stores were affected, but it did not provide a number. One of its stores, in Sjobo in southern Sweden, posted on Facebook that its fridges and freezers had "been hacked and they set the temperature at 50 degrees" Celsius (about 122 degrees Fahrenheit).
"We are looking into what has happened and the scale of it," spokesperson Helena Johansson told AFP, adding that the company was focusing on how to help affected stores.
The Coop chain said six of its around 800 stores in Sweden had problems with their fridges and freezers and had to throw out food, with company spokesman Carlos Cancino telling AFP that the units "either stopped working entirely or have been partially impaired."
"I haven't received any information that this is a cyberattack," he said.
On Oct. 12, major French retailers said hundreds of stores were hit by a cyberattack on their refrigeration systems, which forced them to throw out food and raised concerns about food security. In that incident, refrigeration control systems from Danish manufacturer Danfoss were targeted.
There has been no claim of responsibility for any hack targeting grocery retailers in Europe to date.
Speaking after the French stores were forced to discard thousands of pounds of wasted food last month due to the still-unattributed hack, European Union food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen said in a post on X that "food security requires more attention at all levels," calling the "exploitation" of vulnerabilities in such essential, networked systems a new "reality."
"Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented," Cooperative U CEO Dominique Schelcher wrote on X last month.
Prosecutors in Paris confirmed a cyberattack and said it also hit other major chains and sparked fires as some equipment overheated.

Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Monday. Read our full coverage here.
Iran's 2-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, resume nuclear talks
Iran said it had a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks with the U.S. if Washington meets its demands.
The announcement came as the region braces for possible renewed fighting, even as Iran’s top diplomat said Sunday that he hoped the U.S. would choose “diplomacy over other paths.”
Iran previously said the plan could be implemented within a week if the U.S. met seven conditions, including lifting its blockade of Iranian ports. Iran now says ships passing through the reopened strait would have to follow a route agreed upon by Iran and Oman and travel under Iranian supervision. Separately, Iranian officials have said the U.S. must lift sanctions on Iranian oil sales and agree to a ceasefire that would include Lebanon.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said the plan remained the basis for negotiations with Washington through mediators, despite the shorter implementation timeline. “This once again demonstrates Iran’s good-faith approach,” he added.
Baghaei gave no indication that Tehran had changed its demands or that Washington had accepted its proposal.
President Donald Trump has alternated between pursuing diplomacy and threatening heavy bombing of Iran in his public comments.
More than 300,000 Yemenis have fled fighting, UN says
The U.N. migration agency said the people are struggling to find shelter and life essentials, as aid groups face limited access to those in need.
They have fled as renewed fighting between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed government forces broke a four-year truce, exacerbating an already dire humanitarian situation in one of the Middle East's poorest countries.
Taiz province, in southwestern Yemen, continues to take in displaced families, but many are fleeing south to Aden, which has now received more than 56,000 people, according to the latest figures by the International Organization for Migration.
“After years of conflict, families in Yemen are being forced to flee yet again, often with little more than the clothes on their backs,” Abdusattor Esoev, head of the IOM's mission in Yemen, said Sunday.
“They urgently need shelter, food, clean water and health care. Without more funding, thousands of families could be left without the help they urgently need,” he added.
China to send special envoy to Iran and the Gulf
China said Monday it plans to send a special envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters the envoy would focus on easing tensions and promoting regional stability.
The Gulf region “should not become an arena for great-power rivalry and geopolitical conflict,” Chinese President Xi Jinping told Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq Al Said on Monday, according to a readout of their meeting.
The move comes as China seeks to expand its influence in the rapidly changing region, which it depends on for a large share of its oil.
Two Israeli airstrikes killed two men in southern Gaza early Monday, according to Nasser Hospital, where their bodies were taken. One strike killed a man in his home; the other killed a man in a tent.
The Israeli military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Major fighting between Israel and Hamas largely halted under the October 2025 ceasefire. Israel continues to launch near-daily strikes on Gaza that it says target militants, though the strikes regularly kill or injure women and children. Israel says Hamas uses civilians as human shields.
About 1,580 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire began, bringing the overall death toll to more than 74,500, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, does not distinguish between civilians and militants.

articles.title_orig: Long March leaves its footprints in British libraries
articles.title_zh: Long March leaves its footprints in British libraries
articles.content_orig:
Xinhua |
          Updated: 2026-11-03 08:54
LONDON — In a reading room at the British Library, a blue stamp dated Jan 27, 1937, appears inside a book written by a British missionary who witnessed part of China's Long March.
Nearly 90 years later, the book offers a glimpse into how the extraordinary journey of the Chinese Red Army reached readers thousands of miles away.
As this year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, a remarkable revolutionary feat achieved under the leadership of the Communist Party of China, libraries and archives across Britain, along with the recollections of a writer who retraced the historic route, offer fresh perspectives on a journey that helped shape modern China.
At London's Marx Memorial Library, founded in 1933, two early publications shed light on how the Chinese Red Army was portrayed to British readers.
One is Edgar Snow's Red Star Over China, published in Britain in 1937. Its orange-red cover bears the words "LEFT BOOK CLUB EDITION" and "NOT FOR SALE TO THE PUBLIC".
Snow's account introduced Western readers to the CPC, its leaders and the extraordinary hardships endured by Red Army soldiers during the Long March.
Another is Agnes Smedley's China's Red Army Marches, published in London in 1936. Focusing on the Red Army's activities before its historic journey, the book describes villagers making shoes for soldiers and farmers delivering rice to support them.
One passage even reproduces a revolutionary song, complete with musical notation, preserving the voices of Chinese soldiers in a book published thousands of miles away.
The British Library also holds a 1937 edition of Snow's book bearing a stamp from the former India Office Library dated Oct 30, 1937.
Contemporary British newspapers also reflected growing interest in the Red Army. On Oct 19, 1937, the Edinburgh Evening News published a review of Snow's book, devoting a section specifically to the Long March.
Together, these publications offered British readers accounts of the soldiers' experiences, their daily lives and the circumstances surrounding their remarkable journey, bringing distant events in China into view for the British public.
At the University of East Anglia in Norwich, eastern England, three archival boxes preserve the story of Alfred Bosshardt, a British missionary who accompanied the Red Army through parts of southwestern China.
Bosshardt's experiences were later recounted in The Restraining Hand, published in Britain in 1936, making him one of the earliest Western eyewitnesses to record aspects of the Long March.
The university's collection contains hundreds of items, including correspondence, photographs, newspaper cuttings and audiovisual recordings. Many were collected by British journalist and writer Anthony Grey, who helped bring Bosshardt's story to a wider audience.
Despite their different beliefs, Bosshardt developed considerable respect for the Red Army soldiers, particularly for their discipline and determination.
He recalled that soldiers were instructed to respect villagers, pay for food and compensate residents for damaged property. During breaks from their arduous journey, young soldiers sang songs, wrestled and shared moments of laughter.
Bosshardt also admired Red Army commander Xiao Ke, with whom he later renewed contact. Their friendship continued for decades, forming a remarkable personal link between Britain and China.
Nearly seven decades after the Long March, British-based Chinese writer Sun Shuyun spent 14 months retracing the odyssey. Traveling through remote villages, she interviewed surviving Red Army veterans and their families in an effort to understand the people behind the historical narrative.
For Sun, who studied history at the University of Oxford, the journey became one of the most unforgettable experiences of her life.
In East China's Jiangxi province, she met an elderly woman who had persuaded her newlywed husband to join the Red Army. He never returned. Nearly 70 years later, she was still waiting for him.
In Northwest China's Gansu province, Sun interviewed a former female Red Army soldier whose life had been marked by poverty, captivity and hardship.
The elderly woman welcomed Sun into her home, wrapped her in thick blankets and prepared a meal unusually rich in salt. Her adopted daughter explained that salt had been extremely scarce during the Long March, leaving the woman with a lifelong habit of cherishing it.
Recalling these encounters at her London home, Sun was moved to tears.
She said the Long March demonstrated the CPC's organizational strength and leadership and laid an important foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution.
"The Long March is one of the most important events in modern Chinese history," she said, adding that its legacy continues to resonate with China's development today.
Sun stressed that the choices and sacrifices of ordinary people, whose experiences could sometimes be overlooked in historical narratives, deserve to be remembered and passed down to future generations.
From the hardships of revolutionary struggle to the achievements of modernization, the Chinese people have continued to undertake new journeys requiring courage and perseverance, she said.
The great spirit of the Long March "will always deserve to be remembered", Sun added.

articles.title_orig: PM plans debt re-set for Commonwealth nations as slavery apology talks begin
articles.title_zh: PM plans debt re-set for Commonwealth nations as slavery apology talks begin
articles.content_orig:
The prime minister will join the King at the formal opening of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua later - and begin talks with fellow leaders about the UK issuing a formal apology for the slave trade in the next year.
As part of the discussions, Downing Street said Andy Burnham would set out his plans for what it is calling a "debt reset" to support Commonwealth countries having to deal with the growing costs of paying interest on their debts.
The issue of reparations, compensation to those who were the victims of slavery, has dominated debate in the build up to this summit, in which representatives from 56 Commonwealth countries are meeting.
"Britain is bringing a new approach to this meeting," the prime minister said, in a tacit acknowledgement that the last Commonwealth gathering, on the Pacific island of Samoa two years ago, did not go well from a UK perspective.
The previous Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer had said prior to the meeting that reparations were not on the agenda , but other leaders insisted they should be.
This time, the new prime minister has sought to get ahead of the debate, and appeared to directly address the anger of some Commonwealth leaders after the last summit.
"For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery . By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function," Burnham argued in an article in the Guardian.
Burnham alongside the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and the former Prime Minister Gordon Brown, are beginning conversations which, they hope, will help detoxify the debate about reparations.
They do so while insisting the UK will not pay them, but is likely to formally apologise for the slave trade for the first time next year, when the UK holds the rotating presidency of the G20 group of countries.
"A formal apology," Miliband said in a social media video , is something "the British government are open to".
He said this would be a "significant step" but added that "we don't believe financial reparations are the right or feasible answer to transatlantic slavery. We don't think the right response is to ask British taxpayers today to make financial payments for these historic acts."
The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has urged the prime minister not to issue an apology for slavery, saying it would give countries a reason to ask the UK for reparations.
She said: "I don't think we should be giving any money to compensate people for the slave trade, and I don't think that Andy Burnham needs to be apologising because it is a lever to wedge open the door to ask for cash."
But British officials are hopeful, even confident, that the prime minister and foreign secretary's approach will create space in the next two days for a wider conversation with fellow Commonwealth countries.
No 10 said the UK would lead two new task forces - one focused on critical mineral assets and vulnerabilities in supply chains across the group and the other aimed at boosting trade and investment more widely.
Both will be set up by the end of the year and report back at the next leaders' summit, officials said.
British diplomats view the Commonwealth as a useful forum for conversations with developing countries, and, crucially, one that does not involve China, America or Russia.

Brent crude drops by more than 6% to $105.55 a barrel, the lowest level in more than two weeks
The oil price has fallen to its lowest level in more two weeks amid new hopes of a breakthrough to end the Iran war.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, dropped by more than 6.5% to as low as $105.55 a barrel on Monday, the lowest since 16 October, sending shares in airline companies higher and pushing down government borrowing costs.
Oil prices fell after Tehran revealed that contacts between Iran and the US to end their eight-month war were continuing.
“Consultations through mediators are very ⁠intensive. We have presented our conditions and ⁠proposals and everything depends on the political ​rationality of Washington,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said, according to the state media outlet IRNA.
Over the weekend, Qatari officials tried to negotiate the release of more than $6bn (£4.5bn) in Iranian assets , so that Tehran might allow the strait of Hormuz to reopen.
On Monday, US vice-president JD Vance reported that there had been “a number of good conversations with the Iranians” and that he was feeling good about the prospects of a “negotiated settlement”.
Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, last week but the White House has offered few details about the contents of that correspondence.
Donald Trump had earlier taken a belligerent tone, telling voters in Iowa on Sunday that Iran would receive “the hammer” unless there was progress.
“The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can ... But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer,” he said during a campaign rally in the run-up to the US midterm elections.
But investors were cheered by reports on Monday that Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, had granted “powers” to his government in its talks with the US seeking to end the Middle East war.

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “The news is manna from heaven for stock markets, which have felt increasingly pressured by oil’s rise, but of course there is still a risk that Trump will try one last throw of the iron dice after the midterms.”
The drop in the oil price sparked hopes of a break in the inflationary pressures gripping the global economy. Government borrowing costs dropped, with the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds down 10 basis points, or 0.1 of a percentage point, to the lowest since 22 September.
Shares in British Airways’ parent company, IAG, rose by 4.2% in London, while United Airlines jumped 7% in New York.

articles.title_orig: War, tariffs and China: What the US midterms mean for the Asia-Pacific
articles.title_zh: War, tariffs and China: What the US midterms mean for the Asia-Pacific
articles.content_orig:
Xi urges diplomacy on Iran as Oman’s sultan makes historic visit to China
Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – Across the Asia-Pacific region, governments and businesses reeling from the energy shock of the United States and Israel’s war on Iran are watching Tuesday’s US midterm elections closely.
Many want to see “enormous changes” during the rest of President Donald Trump’s term, analysts say, from the war on Iran to his policies on trade and tariffs. But few expect that to happen, even with the Democrats poised to take the House of Representatives, and potentially the Senate, from Trump’s Republican Party.
“Of course, everybody is watching,” said Steven Okun, a trade specialist and the chief executive of APAC Advisors, a Singapore-based consulting firm. “It’s great political theatre.”
Outside the Middle East, no region has been hit harder by the war on Iran than the Asia-Pacific. Before the start of the conflict in January, the region took in most of the Gulf oil and gas that passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
When Iran closed the chokepoint in response to the US and Israel’s strikes, much of the region was left facing shortages .
The Philippines, which relies on the Gulf for more than 90 percent of its crude oil imports, has been under a national energy emergency since March. Soaring fuel costs have drained the foreign exchange reserves of the region’s poorest economies – Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and East Timor, according to the Institute of Southeast Asian Studies (ISEAS)-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore. Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam have also spent heavily on fuel subsidies to shield consumers, it said.
Public opinion in the Asia-Pacific region remains firmly opposed to the war, but Okun said a Democratic-controlled US Congress was unlikely to force Trump to end the eight-month conflict.
“With Iran, I don’t see [a Democrat-controlled Congress] having much change at all, other than the fact that the war will be investigated and there will be oversight hearings,” Okun told Al Jazeera. “We might even see an impeachment of the secretary of defence, but it doesn’t change the overall impact of the war.”
Under the US Constitution, Congress holds the power to formally declare war, but Trump has claimed the attacks on Iran were in self-defence and has so far ignored congressional resolutions directing him to withdraw US forces from hostilities. If a Democrat-controlled Congress passes legislation restricting military operations or cutting funding for them, Trump can veto it. Overriding a veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers, which Democrats are almost certain to fall short of.
On trade and tariffs, too, analysts see little room for Congress to rein in Trump.
The US president rattled global markets last year when he imposed “reciprocal” tariffs of 10 percent to 50 percent on some 90 countries, with the aim of shrinking the US trade deficit. Asia was again hit harder than most. Cambodia faced a 49 percent tariff and Laos 48 percent. Vietnam was slapped with 46 percent and Myanmar 45 percent.
After the Supreme Court struck down those tariffs in February, the Trump administration turned to other tools . In July, it imposed tariffs of 10 percent and 12.5 percent on goods from 60 trading partners, accusing them of failing to stop imports made with forced labour . In Asia, the list includes China, Japan, South Korea and seven Southeast Asian nations – Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
“In some ways, the new Congress is not going to matter to the Asia Pacific because it’s not going to affect trade policy,” Okun said. “Congress cannot change that … Tariffs don’t change. The war doesn’t change.”
Still, some analysts see a narrow opening.
Stephen Olson, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, argued in a recent essay that a “strong rebuke of ‘Trumpism’” at the polls could embolden a pro-free-trade wing of the Republican Party that has been “intimidated into standing down during the Trump presidency”.
That, Olson wrote, offers “a glimmer of hope” for Southeast Asian countries that depend on the US market. A Democratic-controlled Congress, he said, could also push for carve-outs and exceptions that would give the region’s exporters “a modicum of relief”. But any deeper shift in US trade policy, he added, will have to wait for the 2028 presidential election.
Joshua Kurlantzick, a senior fellow for Southeast Asia and South Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the region’s wish list goes beyond trade to security.
“I think nearly all of Asia would like to see enormous changes, across many domains, during the rest of Trump’s term,” he told Al Jazeera. “But I think much of the region believes this will not happen.”
Besides “more stability” in trade and tariff policy, Asia-Pacific countries “would like to feel more stable in security guarantees from the US,” he said. They would also like a “more clear, obvious US presence” in the South China Sea , where China’s claims overlap with those of five Southeast Asian nations, and in the Taiwan Strait , which separates China from Taiwan , the self-governed island Beijing claims as its territory.
Businesses will also be watching whether a major Republican loss leads to “greater GOP willingness in Congress to stand up to Trump, along with Democrats, on issues important to companies in Asia,” Kurlantzick said, including tariffs, trade policy, arms sales and “overall economic unpredictability”.
One area where analysts do expect some change is US policy on Chinese technology.
The new Congress, whichever party controls it, will pass tougher restrictions on China, said Okun at APAC Advisors.
These include the Remote Access Security Act, which would extend export controls to remote access of US goods, software or technology and the Chip Security Act, which would require companies to verify that advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips remain in authorised locations, to prevent diversion to foreign adversaries. It also includes the Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act, known as the MATCH Act, which would press allies to bring their controls on chipmaking equipment in line with Washington’s, to keep advanced chipmaking technology out of China’s hands.
“The next Congress is going to pass them regardless of midterms because both parties agree on them,” Okun said. “The person who is least restrictive now on China is the US president,” he added, referring to Trump’s courting of China’s President Xi Jinping.
The two men have met twice this year as ties have warmed after a bitter and costly trade war last year. To preserve the fragile trade truce, Trump has also held off approving a $14bn package of arms sales to Taiwan, which would be the largest ever for Taipei.
Some analysts meanwhile worry that a lame-duck Trump, hemmed in at home by a Democratic Congress, could turn more forcefully to foreign policy.
“We should not be surprised by continued erratic foreign policy,” said James Guild, an assistant professor at the Indonesian International Islamic University.
“The Democrats have a poor record of effectively opposing and holding Trump accountable using conventional tools of congressional oversight,” Guild said. “We will have to wait and see if they rise to the moment this time.”
